title: Learning to Choose: Who Are We Becoming?
author: Jennifer W. Shewmaker
summary: Jennifer Shewmaker continues her series on helping students build an ethical framework for their choices about AI by starting with the purpose of the work itself. Prompted by a conference panel on wisdom in the age of AI, she asks what happens when we hand over work without understanding what the work is for. The panel's image of the sorcerer's apprentice, who enchants a broom and then cannot stop it, frames her concern about learners giving away the very work through which they grow. She reports that college students tell her they fear AI will help them finish assignments while leaving them without the understanding they came to develop. Her answer is to root higher education in formation, helping students discover what they are good at and how they can serve their neighbors. The practical move is a question students can ask before using AI: what am I meant to learn by doing this work, and how would AI affect that learning?
points: Students need to understand what an assignment is for before they can make a defensible choice about handing part of it to AI.
The sorcerer's apprentice story illustrates the risk of delegating work whose value lies in the doing, then losing control of the result.
Students already worry that AI may leave them with finished assignments but no understanding, which suggests they want guidance rather than prohibition.
Framing education as formation, becoming someone capable of meaningful work, gives an ethical anchor for AI decisions.
Instructors can start with one reflective question: what do I hope students gain from this assignment, and have I helped them see that purpose?
quotes: What happens when we hand over our work without understanding what that work is actually for?
In education, the effort of working through a question can develop the very understanding we will need later as we apply our knowledge in the real world.
What am I meant to learn by doing this work, and how would using AI affect that learning?
They worry that AI may help them finish assignments while leaving them without the understanding they came to college to develop.
The students bringing these concerns to me want to learn. Their concern is about what they and others might lose if AI does too much of the work for them.

Helping students develop an ethical framework begins here, with the purpose of their learning. Before deciding what to hand over to AI, they need to consider what doing the work could help them become.
